learn.intro: Why would Europeans risk their lives at sea? This topic follows the spice trade, the motives historians sum up as "Gold, God and Glory", and the knowledge and technology, much of it from China, the Islamic world and the Indian Ocean, that made the voyages possible.

sections.title: 1. The spice trade

blocks.p: Pepper, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg and mace grew almost only in South and Southeast Asia. Cloves and nutmeg came from a few small Indonesian islands, the Maluku or "Spice Islands".
Before reaching Europe, spices passed through many hands: Asian producers, Indian Ocean merchants, Arab and Venetian middlemen. Each added a mark-up, so spices were extremely expensive.

Spices were used to flavour and preserve food, in medicine, and to show off wealth. Venice and Genoa grew rich as Europe's gateway for spices. Portugal and Spain had no direct access, so they wanted a sea route that bypassed the middlemen.
Pepper was valuable enough that "peppercorn rent", a token but real payment, is still a phrase in English law today.

evidence: Cloves and nutmeg came from the Maluku (Spice) Islands.
Venice and Genoa controlled Europe's spice gateway.

sections.title: 2. Gold, God and Glory

blocks.p: Historians often group the motives for European voyages under three headings:

ul: GOLD (economic): spices, gold, silver; bypassing middlemen; new markets.
GOD (religious): spreading Christianity. Spain and Portugal were Catholic kingdoms, and the Reconquista ended with the fall of Granada in 1492, the same year as Columbus's voyage.
GLORY (political and personal): rival kingdoms such as Spain and Portugal competed for prestige and land; explorers wanted fame, titles and rewards.

blocks.p: These motives were rarely separate: one voyage could be about wealth, religion and national glory at once. "Spreading Christianity" was also used to justify conquest and forced conversion, which later lessons examine.

evidence: Granada fell in 1492, ending the Reconquista.

sections.title: 3. Borrowed knowledge

blocks.p: European ocean voyages depended on knowledge and technology that mostly did not begin in Europe:

ul: The magnetic compass was developed in China by about the 11th century.
The astrolabe, used to work out latitude from the stars, was refined by Islamic astronomers, building on Greek work.
Islamic scholars preserved and advanced Greek geography and astronomy.
Arab, Gujarati and East African pilots knew the Indian Ocean's monsoons, currents and coasts; da Gama used a local pilot for the last leg to India in 1498.
The caravel combined a European hull with the triangular lateen sail long used in the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean, helping ships sail against the wind.

blocks.p: A popular claim says the navigator Ahmad ibn Majid guided da Gama to India. Historians dispute this, so treat it as a claim to check, not a settled fact.

evidence: Da Gama used a local pilot from East Africa to India in 1498.

timeline.event: The magnetic compass is in use in China.
Bartolomeu Dias sails round the Cape of Good Hope.
The Treaty of Tordesillas divides newly claimed lands between Spain and Portugal.
Vasco da Gama reaches India with the help of a local pilot.

people.name: Prince Henry "the Navigator"
people.role: Portuguese prince (1394–1460) who sponsored early voyages down the African coast.

people.name: Ahmad ibn Majid
people.role: Famous Arab navigator; the claim that he guided da Gama is disputed.

people.name: Bartolomeu Dias
people.role: Portuguese sailor who rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488.

vocab.def: A raw material or product bought and sold.
Someone who buys and sells goods for profit.
Total control of the trade in a particular good.
A trader who buys from producers and sells on.
The relationship between causes and their effects.
Planning and following a course, especially at sea.
Instrument measuring star positions, used for navigation.
A small, fast Portuguese sailing ship.

misconceptions.wrong: Spices were mainly used to hide rotten meat.
misconceptions.right: They were used for flavour, preserving, medicine and as a status symbol.
Gold, God and Glory usually worked together.

misconceptions.wrong: European technology made the voyages possible on its own.
misconceptions.right: Much of it came from China, the Islamic world and the Indian Ocean.

misconceptions.wrong: Ahmad ibn Majid definitely guided da Gama.
misconceptions.right: This is a disputed claim, not a settled fact.

sources.title: An Islamic astrolabe
sources.date: Made between about the 10th and 15th centuries
sources.origin: Islamic world; examples are held by the British Museum and the History of Science Museum, Oxford.
sources.purpose: To measure the positions of stars for time-keeping, prayer times and navigation.
sources.usefulness: Physical evidence of advanced Islamic science. One object cannot show how widely it was used at sea.

evidence.q: Explain why Portugal and Spain wanted a sea route to Asia.
evidence.model: Spices reached Europe through Venetian and Arab middlemen who each added a mark-up. A direct sea route would let Portugal and Spain bypass them and take the profit themselves.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that European voyages relied on knowledge from beyond Europe.
evidence.model: The compass came from China, the astrolabe was refined by Islamic astronomers, and da Gama used a local pilot for the final leg to India in 1498.

checklist.text: I can describe how spices travelled from Asia to Europe.
I can describe the three motives: Gold, God and Glory.
I can explain why spices were so expensive in Europe.
I can explain how knowledge from beyond Europe made the voyages possible.
I can judge which motive was most important, recognising they overlapped.
I can judge whether "borrowed knowledge" changes how significant European voyages were.

exam.criteria_note: Practice questions written for this unit. AI feedback is formative only (no marks) until department KS3 criteria are added.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Gold was the main reason Europeans travelled further." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh the economic motive against God and Glory, and recognise how they overlapped.
steps: Explain the gold/economic motive with spice evidence.
Explain at least one other motive with evidence.
Judge, using a qualifier, and say how they linked.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.
mistakes: Choosing one motive and ignoring the others

full: P: Gold was to a large / some extent the main reason because…
E: For example, spices passed through…
E: This meant that… However, God / Glory…
some: P: qualified claim (highly / partly / to some extent…)
E: precise evidence (name, date, number, source)
E: explain with a connective (because / this meant that / therefore)
J: judgement that answers the question

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: Explain how knowledge from beyond Europe made European voyages possible.
questions.asks: Explain at least two examples of borrowed knowledge or technology and how each helped.
steps: Choose two examples (compass, astrolabe, pilots, lateen sail).
Explain how it helped ships sail further.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 7 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

full: P: Knowledge from beyond Europe was highly important because…
E: For example, the compass from China…
E: This meant that… As a result…
some: P: qualified claim (highly / partly / to some extent…)
E: precise evidence (name, date, number, source)
E: explain with a connective (because / this meant that / therefore)
J: judgement that answers the question

stretch.task: If spices were expensive mainly because of the middlemen, did their price reflect how useful they were, or something else?
Is Gold, God and Glory too simple a model for why people do things? Suggest a better model.
If Europeans depended on Chinese, Islamic and Indian Ocean knowledge, does that change how significant their voyages were, or just how we explain them?
Research the Ahmad ibn Majid story. What evidence would you need to decide whether it is true?
